pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 7–9; understand how energy/nutrients flow through a rainforest food web — producers (plants) → primary consumers (herbivores) → secondary consumers (predators) — and that decomposers (fungi, insects) break down dead material and recycle nutrients back to the soil.
• Standards — UK: DfE KS2 Y4 'Living things and their habitats' (construct and interpret food chains; identify producers, predators and prey) — the exploratory age-7 lead-in to that Y4 node.
• Standards — US: NGSS 5-LS2-1 (matter/energy movement among plants, animals, decomposers, environment) and 5-PS3-1 (energy from food traces back to the Sun).
• Operational details — build the chain in the correct DIRECTION with arrows meaning 'energy flows TO': Sun → kapok leaves → leaf-cutter ant → anteater → jaguar. Introduce the three roles with clear tests: producer MAKES its own food (photosynthesis), consumer EATS others, decomposer BREAKS DOWN the dead. Show the web (many interlinked chains) not just one chain, and close the loop with decomposers returning nutrients to the soil for producers. Emphasise arrow direction as the classic error.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (7): build a 3-level chain producer→herbivore→predator with arrows the right way. Tier B (8): explain the decomposer's role in returning nutrients to soil. Tier C (9): use producer/consumer/decomposer correctly and predict a knock-on effect when one species is removed from the web.
bestPractices: Insist on correct arrow direction — arrows point TO the eater, showing where energy flows — as this is the classic error.
Teach the three roles by test, not label: producer MAKES food, consumer EATS others, decomposer BREAKS DOWN the dead.
Move from a single chain to an interconnected WEB so interdependence is visible.
Close the loop: decomposers return nutrients to soil for producers — the recycling that leads into the Y5/6 nutrient-cycling topic.
Use remove-a-species reasoning to reveal knock-on effects and the fragility of the web.
keyRepresentations: A directional food chain Sun→plant→herbivore→predator with energy-flow arrows.
A multi-strand food WEB linking several chains.
A closed nutrient loop: dead matter → decomposers → soil → roots.
commonMisconceptions: 'Arrows point to who eats / to the prey' — arrows show energy flow, pointing toward the consumer.
'Decomposers are just rubbish/dead things' — they are active organisms that recycle nutrients.
'Big predators are producers because they're at the top' — confusing trophic position; only plants are producers.
'Removing one animal doesn't matter' — webs are interdependent; one loss can cascade.
'Energy is recycled like nutrients' — nutrients cycle, but energy flows one way from the Sun and is lost as heat.

learn.summary: For learners aged 7–9, build understanding of a rainforest food web: energy flows from producers (plants) to primary consumers (herbivores) to secondary consumers (predators), while decomposers (fungi, insects) break down dead material and recycle nutrients back to the soil. Core teaching goals are correct arrow direction (arrows mean 'energy flows TO the eater'), defining the three roles by test rather than label, moving from a single chain to an interconnected web, and reasoning about knock-on effects when a species is removed. A build-and-perturb activity is the lead approach, with a labelled reference web and sequence/matching tasks as complementary supports. Energy flows one way from the Sun and is lost as heat; only nutrients cycle.

activities.title: Build the web, then pull a thread
feedback: If an arrow points from the eater to its food, prompt: 'The arrow means energy flows TO — which way does the food (energy) go?' and let the learner flip it toward the eater.
If the learner builds a chain with no decomposers, prompt them to add fungi/insects that break down the dead material and return nutrients to the soil, closing the loop.
If the learner treats a plant as an eater or gives it a food source, remind them plants are producers that make their own food from sunlight and start the chain.

After removing the ants, draw attention to the fading anteater (in this model the ants are its only food) and then the thinning jaguar (it has lost the anteater it preys on here), so the cascade along the chain is seen rather than just stated. Mention that real anteaters and jaguars have other food too.
activities.rationale: A build-and-perturb system lets the learner construct chains, test arrow direction, and watch a cascade when a species is removed; it is intended to make the 'arrows = energy flow' rule and web interdependence experienced rather than only memorised. Live recomputation when a species is removed targets the common belief that removing one animal doesn't matter. This supports KS2 Y4 construction/interpretation of food chains and NGSS 5-LS2-1 energy/matter movement. Efficacy relative to other media is not established here.
sourceClaims: KS2 Y4 pupils construct and interpret a variety of food chains, identifying producers, predators and prey
Energy flows from producers to consumers and decomposers recycle nutrients from dead material back into the soil; arrows in a food chain denote the direction of energy/matter flow
learnerActions: Assemble a rainforest food web by placing the energy source and organisms: sunlight (the Sun), kapok leaves, a leaf-cutter ant, an anteater, a jaguar, and fungi on the forest floor.
Draw energy-flow arrows between them in the correct direction, starting Sun → kapok leaves → leaf-cutter ant → anteater → jaguar.
When you draw an arrow the wrong way (e.g. from the anteater TO the ant), respond to the prompt 'which way does the FOOD (energy) go?' and flip it to point toward the eater.
Connect the dead jaguar and fallen leaf litter to the fungi, and the fungi back to the soil and roots, closing the nutrient loop.

Remove the leaf-cutter ants from the web and observe what happens in this simplified model to the anteater (which eats the ants) and then the jaguar (which eats the anteater), so the cascade along the chain is visible. In a real rainforest, these animals also eat other food, so the effect would usually be smaller.
Explain in your own words why pulling out one species affects the others.
activities.intendedInsight: Producers, consumers and decomposers are not just a list of labels — they are connected to each other. Energy flows one way from the Sun toward each eater and is not recycled, while nutrients cycle back through decomposers to the soil for plants to reuse. Removing one species can affect others that depend on it, and the effect can pass along a chain.

activities.title: Label the web: roles and who eats whom
feedback: If a learner calls a top predator a 'producer' because it is at the top, apply the test: does it make its own food? In this web only the plants do, so the jaguar is a consumer.
If the learner thinks decomposers are 'just rubbish or dead things', clarify they are active organisms that recycle nutrients back into the soil.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal reference diagram supports vocabulary and layout and works alongside the construction activity. On its own it lets a learner read and identify roles but does not elicit testing of arrow direction or observing a cascade, so it is best used as a companion reference rather than a replacement for building.
sourceClaims: KS2 Y4 pupils construct and interpret a variety of food chains, identifying producers, predators and prey
learnerActions: Explore a labelled rainforest web diagram where tapping an organism reveals its role (producer, consumer or decomposer) and what eats it.
Use each role's TEST to justify the label: producer MAKES its own food by photosynthesis, consumer EATS others, decomposer BREAKS DOWN the dead.
Trace at least one full chain through the web and read the layout of the many interlinked chains.
activities.intendedInsight: The vocabulary (producer, consumer, decomposer) and web layout become a clear reference, defined by what each organism DOES rather than just a name or its position in the diagram.

activities.title: Order the chain and sort the roles
feedback: If a chain is ordered with a predator before its prey, ask what each organism eats and rebuild from the producer outward.
If an arrow is reversed, re-state that arrows point to the eater because they show where energy flows.

A sorting-and-ordering task can check classification and sequence, but it does not itself show interdependence — follow with the build-and-perturb activity to see how the sorted organisms connect and depend on each other.
activities.rationale: Sequence and matching tasks map directly onto the evidence statements and give a clean check of ordering and vocabulary. Such a task assesses recognition and ordering but does not display the interdependence cascade, so it complements rather than replaces construction.
sourceClaims: KS2 Y4 pupils construct and interpret a variety of food chains, identifying producers, predators and prey
learnerActions: Order a scrambled set of organisms into a correct chain (producer → herbivore → predator), placing an arrow at each link pointing toward the eater.
Sort a mixed set of rainforest organisms into producers, consumers and decomposers.
State for each sorted organism the test that justifies its group (makes food / eats others / breaks down the dead).
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to order a chain with correct arrows and categorise organisms by role confirms the vocabulary and sequencing are secure.

constraints: Insist on correct arrow direction: arrows point TO the eater, showing where energy flows. This is the classic learner error and should be checked explicitly.
Teach the three roles by test, not label: producer MAKES food, consumer EATS others, decomposer BREAKS DOWN the dead.
Move from a single chain to an interconnected web so interdependence is visible, and close the loop with decomposers returning nutrients to the soil for producers.

Keep the consumer and decomposer roles distinct in the removal cascade: in this simplified model, removing a consumer (the leaf-cutter ant) can propagate along the chain (anteater, then jaguar). In a real rainforest the effect is usually smaller, because anteaters eat many kinds of ants and termites and jaguars hunt many prey. In this web the fungi, not the leaf-cutter ants, are the decomposers that recycle dead leaf litter.

Distinguish nutrient cycling (nutrients return to the soil and are reused) from energy flow (energy flows one way from the Sun and is lost as heat; it is not recycled). Avoid implying energy is recycled.

A tap-to-reveal reference diagram and sequence/matching tasks support vocabulary and ordering; by themselves they do not elicit testing of arrow direction or experiencing a cascade, so use them alongside construction, not instead of it.

Checkpoint tiers: Tier A (age 7) build a 3-level chain producer→herbivore→predator with arrows the right way; Tier B (age 8) explain the decomposer's role in returning nutrients to soil; Tier C (age 9) use producer/consumer/decomposer correctly and predict a knock-on effect when one species is removed.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; both cited sources carry verified:false in the source row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The two listed sources were not re-fetched; citations support the teaching principles (chain construction, energy/matter flow direction, decomposer recycling) but do not establish that these specific activities were tested or that any one medium is superior.

The original 3D and conversation 'poor fit' judgements (e.g. '3D adds nothing', concept 'better done than discussed') were catalog-preference rankings and are not carried as universal claims; a relational web fits a 2D build, but necessity of any one medium is not established.
Efficacy phrasing ('FELT rather than memorised') was softened to intended-effect wording, since comparative efficacy is not established by the sources.

The original recommendation described leaf litter 'piling up unrecycled' when the leaf-cutter ants were removed. Because leaf-cutter ants are consumers rather than the litter's recyclers, this is ecologically misleading and has been removed from the learner-facing cascade; decomposer fungi remain the litter recyclers in the closed-loop step. The learner-facing cascade is now the clean ant → anteater → jaguar chain.

probeDeeper: What do we call a plant's role in a food chain — producer, consumer or decomposer?
What would happen to the forest if all the decomposers disappeared?
Build me a rainforest chain with at least three links, using an arrow each time.
If the caterpillars all vanished, what happens to the birds that eat them, and to the leaves? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: The arrow points FROM the leaf TO the caterpillar. The arrow shows which way the energy (food) flows — from the thing being eaten to the eater — so it always points towards the animal doing the eating: leaf → caterpillar → bird, and so on. Decomposers like fungi and insects then break down dead things and return the nutrients to the soil for plants to use again.

errorPatterns.pattern: the arrow points to the food/prey — 'it points at what gets eaten'
errorPatterns.nextMove: the arrow means 'energy flows to'; it points to the EATER, from food to feeder
errorPatterns.distractor: From the caterpillar to the leaf, because the arrow points at its food
errorPatterns.revealedBy: draws the arrow from the caterpillar to the leaf

errorPatterns.pattern: decomposers are ignored / not part of the web — 'fungi aren't in the food chain'
errorPatterns.nextMove: add decomposers returning nutrients to the soil, closing the loop
errorPatterns.revealedBy: builds a chain with no decomposers or role for dead material

errorPatterns.pattern: plants get their food by eating, like animals — doesn't see plants as producers
errorPatterns.nextMove: plants are producers; they make their own food from sunlight and start the chain
errorPatterns.revealedBy: places a plant as a consumer or gives it a food source

responseLevels.gap: Points the arrow at the food; treats plants as eaters; no decomposers.
responseLevels.full: Draws arrows from food to eater to show energy flow, builds a 3+ level chain using producer/consumer/decomposer correctly, and explains decomposers recycling nutrients to the soil.
responseLevels.partial: Builds a chain and mostly points arrows correctly but can't explain they show energy flow, or omits decomposers.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In a food chain we draw an arrow between a leaf and a caterpillar that eats it. Which way should the arrow point — from the leaf to the caterpillar, or from the caterpillar to the leaf? Draw it, and then tell me WHY it points that way.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks the arrow points to the food ('the caterpillar wants the leaf') reverses it; the concept child knows the arrow tracks energy flow toward the eater. The reason-tier forces the energy-flow meaning.
